column4: This is the section's stated cycle: charity from property purifies the giver, then the Prophet's prayer (salli ʿalayhim) is “sakanun lahum”; it joins giving, tazkiyah, and reassurance in one act.
The section links property given to a prayer that settles its recipients; here the Bedouins' expenditures are “qurubāt” and the Messenger's prayers are named as a further nearness to God.
The section makes prayer answer outwardly in aid: this account of al-birr joins giving wealth to kin, orphans, and the miskīn with prayer and zakāh, making those acts one lived righteousness.

The section says the prayer's social face is severed when the share is withheld; this description of hypocrites pairs their reluctant prayer with reluctant spending and shows the same split as deliberate hypocrisy.
The section's poor, prayer, and charity belong together; this covenant names parents, kin, orphans, the miskīn, prayer, and zakāh, then says most turned away, a direct breach of that relation.

The source's root ص ل و includes bounded ritual prayer, and the section argues that it reaches the use of wealth; Shuʿayb's opponents ask whether his prayer commands them to change how they deal with their property.
The source distinguishes ritual ṣalāh from its outward benefit; Jesus says he was enjoined with ṣalāh and zakāh for as long as he lives, joining worship to material duty.

The section's men keep the name of prayer while failing the needy; in the answer about Saqar, the condemned say they were not among those who prayed, and 74:44 adds that they did not feed the miskīn, setting true prayer beside care for the poor.

The section treats the hungry person's unmet need as the break in prayer's outward reach; this answer names “feeding the miskīn” as a reason for ruin, while 74:43 supplies the companion failure to pray.
The section's 107:3 background is the failure to urge food for the poor; this rebuke says they do not urge one another to feed the miskīn, making the lost social obligation explicit.
The section traces property given toward a needy person; here the righteous give food to the miskīn, orphan, and captive despite loving it, embodying the outward generosity its hypocrites withhold.

The section contrasts worship turned toward spectators with a prayer meant to benefit another; these feeders say they seek God's face and want neither repayment nor thanks, clarifying the motive behind 76:8's gift.
The section's charity should purify and calm its recipient; this passage says spending loses its merit when followed by reminders or injury, guarding the receiver from the donor's self-display.
The section understands prayer as a comforting word directed to people; here a good word and pardon are better than charity followed by hurt, making the manner of giving part of its benefit.

The section condemns a prayer aimed at being seen while withholding help; this warning explicitly pairs charity ruined by injury with spending for “riyāʾ al-nās,” exposing the same audience-facing piety.
The section's spectacle-facing prayer leaves the needy without its benefit; this verse describes those who spend to be seen by people, linking ostentation directly to the use of wealth.
The section's Tevbe 9:103 says charity purifies its giver; this person “yuʾtī mālahu yatazakkā,” giving wealth in order to purify himself, a direct parallel to that cycle.
The section warns that prayer performed for spectators has lost its outward purpose; this verse says he seeks only his Lord's face, supplying the opposite audience for giving.
The section presents charity as a purifying gift received by God; this neighbor to 9:103 says God accepts repentance and takes the charities, completing the divine side of the transfer.
The section's prayer-and-giving cycle ends at the poor; this verse names the miskīn among the recipients of obligatory charities, making the transfer's destination concrete.

The section says worship has a face turned toward other people; here believing men and women are each other's allies, maintain prayer, give zakāh, and seek God's mercy, placing the paired acts in mutual care.
The section's giver sets aside a share instead of hoarding it; these believers prefer others over themselves even in need, and the verse calls success freedom from the soul's stinginess.
The section says the needy should receive what the worshipper withholds; this account of the God-fearing says their property contains a due for the asker and the deprived.

The section condemns people heedless about their ṣalāh; this passage describes people constant in ṣalāh, and 70:24–25 immediately show that their constancy includes a known due for the asker and deprived.

The section's cycle moves from worship to a portion of wealth for someone else; this passage gives the constant worshippers a “known due” in their property, and 70:25 identifies its recipients as asker and deprived.
The section connects prayer with the miskīn's unmet need; this verse names the asker and deprived as recipients of a known claim on the worshippers' property, specified in 70:24.
The section condemns prayer staged for sight; here giving charity openly is good but concealing it and giving it to the poor is better, and it erases sins, directing wealth away from display.
The section contrasts looking for an audience with care for another; this verse says expenditure for the poor is for the giver's own good and describes giving while seeking God's face.
The section connects property, the miskīn, and seeking divine acceptance; this verse assigns the poor and traveler their due and says this is best for those seeking God's face.

The section says the prayer's outward reach should meet need; this command assigns kin, the miskīn, and the traveler their due, naming concrete recipients of the wealth that the section's worshippers withhold.
The section's giving cycle needs a recipient; asked what to spend, this verse names parents, kin, orphans, the miskīn, and travelers as those who should receive good expenditure.
The section's hungry person is left without the aid that should issue from worship; this verse names feeding on a day of hunger as the needed act.
The section connects the miskīn to nourishment and a share of wealth; this verse identifies a “miskīnan dhā matrabah,” a poor person in the dust.
The section's charity purifies its giver; this verse says one will not attain al-birr until spending from what one loves, tying costly generosity to moral worth.

The section describes people withholding what should reach others; here, after receiving God's bounty, people are said to have withheld it and turned away, a specific reversal of the charitable cycle.

The section describes prayer emptied of sincerity; this neighbor to 9:76 says their broken pledge and lies left hypocrisy in their hearts, naming the inward consequence of withholding after a promise.

The section's hypocrites close their social hand while retaining religious appearance; this description of hypocrite men and women says they close their hands and forget God, a direct likeness of withholding help.
The section says property should move to the needy rather than be withheld; this warning targets those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way.
The source's root ص ل و includes formal prayer, whose inner orientation the section says is missing; these successful believers are humble in their prayers, the opposite of heedlessness.
The section joins prayer's inward purpose to giving; this portrait places zakāh among the deeds of successful believers, between turning from idle speech and guarding chastity.
The section condemns being heedless about ṣalāh; this portrait closes by saying successful believers guard their prayers, a direct reversal of that neglect.
The section distinguishes real prayer from a hollow outward act; this verse says later people lost ṣalāh and followed desires, giving the inward failure its consequence.
The section asks what prayer does within a person; this verse says ṣalāh restrains indecency and wrong, stating the moral work that the hollow worshippers have lost.
The section's action releases wealth to bring purification and peace; this opposing portrait joins miserliness with thinking oneself self-sufficient, the stance that closes off the transfer.
The section says ṣalāh and charity are bound to social obligation; this verse makes repentance, maintaining prayer, and giving zakāh the condition for becoming brothers in religion.
The section's ṣalāh is tested by its relation to the community; this verse describes God's mosques as maintained by those who believe, establish prayer, and give zakāh.
The section connects worship to how wealth is handled; this verse says trade and sale do not distract believers from remembrance, prayer, and zakāh, directly setting commerce beside worship.
The section's cycle joins prayer and giving to reassurance; this verse commands prayer, zakāh, and obedience to the Messenger, then points to receiving mercy.
The section contrasts prayer meant for spectators with prayer's true purpose; this verse frames worship as sincere devotion and pairs establishing prayer with giving zakāh.
The section makes worship issue in generosity; this description of believers pairs establishing prayer with spending from what God has provided them.
The section links prayer with property reaching others; this account pairs establishing prayer with spending secretly and openly from provision, and says they answer evil with good.
The section's charity is a share sent beyond the self; this command pairs prayer with spending, secretly and openly, before a day without trade or friendship.
The section treats worship as a communal practice with material consequences; this portrait of believers pairs prayer and spending from their provision with consultation over their affairs.
The section joins prayer to the use of property; this verse pairs prayer with secret and public expenditure and calls it a trade that will not perish.
The section argues that ṣalāh reaches beyond private performance; Ishmael is praised for ordering his family to prayer and zakāh, carrying worship into household conduct.
The section joins worship to active care; the guided leaders are described as doing good, establishing prayer, and giving zakāh, so the pair belongs to lived guidance.
The section says worship must shape treatment of others; those established in the land are described as maintaining prayer and zakāh while enjoining right and forbidding wrong.
The source's root ص ل و includes bounded ritual worship; this command pairs establishing ṣalāh with zakāh and communal bowing, placing formal prayer beside material duty.
The section links ṣalāh to good that reaches beyond the worshipper; this command pairs prayer and zakāh with any good sent ahead to be found with God.
The section's prayer and gift are presented as one faithful practice; this verse pairs prayer and zakāh with a promise that the faithful need not fear or grieve.
The source distinguishes God's ṣalāh as purification or blessing; here God's ṣalawāt and mercy come upon the patient, giving a divine response that comforts those enduring hardship.
The source's root ص ل و includes God's ṣalāh as an act of cleansing; this verse says God and the angels send ṣalāh on believers to bring them from darkness into light.
The source distinguishes human prayer from God's action of ṣalāh; this verse commands believers themselves to send ṣalāh on the Prophet, showing the word's interpersonal use beyond ritual prayer.

The source's dictionary gloss for س ك ن is whatever beloved thing one finds rest in; this verse says spouses are created so each may find tranquility with the other, extending that relational comfort beyond the charity scene.
The section says the Prophet's prayer gives people repose; this verse describes hearts finding rest in remembering God, a nonlexical counterpart for how reassurance settles the inward person.

The source's root س ك ن links the needy person with repose; after battle panic, this verse says God sent sakīnah upon His Messenger and the believers, a parallel picture of reassurance arriving to people.
The section treats sakan as calm given to another; this verse says God sent sakīnah upon His Messenger in the cave, a divine reassurance rather than a human prayer.
The source's root س ك ن links the miskīn with repose; this verse says God sends sakīnah into believers' hearts, a parallel account of calm settling within a community.
The section's “sakanun lahum” makes tranquility a gift to people; this verse says God sent sakīnah upon the believers at the pledge, echoing reassurance in a communal bond.

The section asks that the miskīn receive what prayer should move a person to give; this verse depicts poor people devoted to God's way who need support but are mistaken for self-sufficient because of their restraint.

The section condemns worshippers who withhold what should reach the poor; this verse says people love wealth intensely, supplying the inward attachment behind refusal to urge food for the miskīn in 89:18.
The section's cycle turns worship toward the miskīn, while this account of the denier says he did not urge feeding the poor; it states the same failed social duty as a cause of ruin.
The section says the prayerful should not withhold what reaches the needy; these garden owners agree to keep a poor person from entering their harvest, staging that refusal as a deliberate act.
The section's hypocrites retain a religious appearance but withhold aid; this portrait says people hold back when good reaches them, then immediately sets the praying people apart.

The section says prayer's inward and outward sides have been split; this verse makes the praying people an exception to withholding (70:21), and 70:23–25 specify their constancy and the due in their property.
The source distinguishes ritual ṣalāh from supplication; Ibrahim asks to be made an establisher of prayer and then asks God to accept his duʿāʾ, putting both directions in one plea.

The section says the Prophet's prayer should bring its recipients tranquility; this account of charity recipients says they rejoice if given a share but become angry if not, showing the self-interested response the cycle must overcome.
The section links an inward state of worship to spending for others; this portrait joins trembling hearts, patience, prayer, and spending from God's provision in the same description of the faithful.
The section sends a share of property toward people in need; this rule for distributing communal wealth names the poor and other recipients and says it should not circulate only among the rich.
The section says charity purifies the giver; this verse pictures spending to seek God's approval as a fruitful garden, directly contrasting the preceding warning against showy, harmful charity.
The section condemns withholding the share due to others; facing death, a person regrets delay and asks to give charity and become righteous, showing the lost opportunity to give.
The section's worshippers keep property from others; this verse describes misers who urge miserliness and conceal God's bounty, a direct reversal of the outward gift that should accompany prayer.
The section connects a material gift to reassurance; this verse describes people spending by night and day, secretly and openly, and promises them no fear or grief.
The section treats prayer as inseparable from duties to people; this command to worship God is followed by kindness to relatives, orphans, the miskīn, and neighbors.

The section's prayer has a face directed toward other people; this verse identifies charitable giving, good conduct, or reconciliation as the few kinds of private counsel that are good when done seeking God's approval.

The section develops the source's root س ك ن as relational settling and repose; Ibrahim says he settled descendants near the sacred house so they may pray, then asks that hearts incline toward them and provision reach them.

The section exposes piety performed for an audience; here hypocrites mock believers who contribute generously or can offer only little, showing how public judgment can attack the very giving the section calls for.

The section presents expenditure as a path to nearness and tranquility; these Bedouins regard what they spend as a fine and expect harm to befall the believers, a specific contrary stance toward giving.
The section makes giving part of worship's effect on relationships; this portrait of the God-conscious joins spending in ease and hardship with restraining anger and pardoning people.
The section links giving wealth with purification; this verse describes charitable men and women and those who lend God a good loan, making material generosity an act of worship.
The source's root ص ل و denotes ritual prayer in one branch, while the section joins it to the zakāh represented by Maʿūn; this verse pairs prayer and zakāh with a good loan to God.
The section says prayer and giving cannot be separated; in this post-conflict boundary, repentance, establishing prayer, and giving zakāh precede release from hostilities.

The section's positive cycle begins with giving and ends in purification and reassurance; this verse's contrasting portrait is of one who gives and is mindful of God, the charitable path set against the miser in 92:8.
